# Problem 1

## Data import and description

```{r}

data("ny_noaa")

dim(ny_noaa)


```

The `ny_noaa` dataset contains 2,595,176 observations and 7 variables. It includes daily meteorological observations from weather stations across New York State.

Key variables include station ID (`id`), observation date (`date`), precipitation (`prcp`), snowfall (`snow`), snow depth (`snwd`), maximum temperature (`tmax`), and minimum temperature (`tmin`).


```{r noaa-missing}
missing_summary = ny_noaa |>
  summarize(
    across(
      everything(),
      ~ sum(is.na(.x))
    )
  )

missing_summary
```


```{r noaa-missing-percent}
missing_percent = ny_noaa |>
  summarize(
    across(
      everything(),
      ~ mean(is.na(.x)) * 100
    )
  )

missing_percent
```

The `ny_noaa` dataset contains 2,595,176 observations and 7 variables. It includes daily weather records from weather stations across New York State.

The key variables include station ID (`id`), date (`date`), precipitation (`prcp`), snowfall (`snow`), snow depth (`snwd`), maximum temperature (`tmax`), and minimum temperature (`tmin`).

Missing values are present in several weather variables. In particular, missing temperature measurements may affect the analysis of daily maximum and minimum temperatures. Missing observations will be handled appropriately when calculating summaries and producing visualizations.

## Data cleaning

```{r noaa-cleaning}
noaa_clean = ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    year = lubridate::year(date),
    month = lubridate::month(date),
    day = lubridate::day(date),
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,
    prcp = prcp / 10
  )

glimpse(noaa_clean)
```

```{r snowfall-frequency}
snow_frequency = noaa_clean |>
  count(snow, sort = TRUE)

head(snow_frequency, 10)
```


```{r snowfall-observed}
noaa_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(snow)) |>
  count(snow, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(10)
```
The most common snowfall value is 0 mm, with 2,008,508 observations. The next most common values are 25 mm, 13 mm, and 51 mm. This makes sense because most days have no snowfall. The dataset also contains 381,221 missing snowfall observations.
## Average maximum temperature in January and July

```{r temperature-summary}
noaa_temp = noaa_clean |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(!is.nan(mean_tmax))

head(noaa_temp)
```

```{r january-july-temperature}
noaa_temp |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3, color = "steelblue") +
  facet_grid(. ~ month,
             labeller = as_labeller(
               c(`1` = "January", `7` = "July")
             )) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Maximum Temperature by Station",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average Maximum Temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
Average maximum temperatures are much higher in July than in January. January temperatures vary more across years, while July temperatures are relatively stable. There are also a few unusual values, especially in July, where some stations have much lower average temperatures than the others. Overall, there is no clear long-term increasing or decreasing trend.

## Temperature relationship and snowfall distribution

```{r temperature-relationship}
temp_plot = noaa_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(tmax), !is.na(tmin)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_bin2d(bins = 50) +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum vs Minimum Temperature",
    x = "Minimum Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum Temperature (°C)",
    fill = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

temp_plot
```

```{r snowfall-distribution}
snow_plot = noaa_clean |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = snow)) +
  geom_boxplot(
    fill = "lightblue",
    outlier.alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall Distribution by Year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall (mm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 90,
      hjust = 1
    )
  )

snow_plot
```


```{r combined-weather-plots-final, fig.width=12, fig.height=5, out.width="100%"}
(temp_plot | snow_plot) +
  patchwork::plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1.5))

```
There is a clear positive relationship between minimum and maximum temperatures. As minimum temperature increases, maximum temperature also tends to increase. Most observations are concentrated in the middle of the plot, with a few extreme values.Snowfall distributions are similar across most years. The median snowfall is around 25 mm, and the middle 50% of observations generally falls between about 13 and 51 mm. Some years, such as 2006 and 2010, show somewhat different distributions. There is no obvious long-term trend in the snowfall amounts shown.

# Problem 2

## Data import and cleaning


```{r nhanes-cleaning}
nhanes_covar = read_csv(
  "data/nhanes_covar.csv",
  skip = 4
) |>
  janitor::clean_names()

nhanes_accel = read_csv(
  "data/nhanes_accel.csv"
) |>
  janitor::clean_names()

nhanes_data = nhanes_covar |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  drop_na(sex, age, bmi, education) |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c(
        "Less than high school",
        "High school equivalent",
        "More than high school"
      )
    )
  ) |>
  inner_join(nhanes_accel, by = "seqn")

nhanes_data |>
  select(seqn, sex, age, bmi, education) |>
  head()
```
The NHANES demographic and accelerometer datasets were combined using participant ID (SEQN). Participants under 21 years old and those with missing demographic information were excluded. Sex and education were converted into categorical variables for further analysis.

## Demographic characteristics

```{r nhanes-demographics}
nhanes_data |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "Number of participants by sex and education"
  )
```

The more than high school group has the largest number of participants, with 56 males and 59 females. The less than high school group has similar numbers of males and females, while the high school equivalent group has more males than females.

```{r nhanes-age-distribution}
nhanes_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distribution by Sex and Education",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
The age distributions vary across education groups. In the more than high school group, females have a noticeable peak around ages 30–40. The other two education groups show more spread across ages. Overall, the age distributions of males and females overlap, but there are some differences between the groups.
## Total Daily Activity

```{r nhanes-total-activity}
nhanes_long = nhanes_data |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = matches("^min[0-9]+$"),
    names_to = "minute",
    values_to = "mims"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    minute = as.numeric(
      stringr::str_remove(minute, "min")
    ) - 1
  )

nhanes_total = nhanes_long |>
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, education) |>
  summarize(
    total_activity = sum(mims, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r nhanes-total-plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
nhanes_total |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = age,
    y = total_activity,
    color = sex
  )) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Daily Activity by Age",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total Activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
Total daily activity generally decreases with age, although there is considerable variation among participants. The patterns differ somewhat between males and females across education groups. In the high school equivalent group, females show higher activity levels than males around ages 40–50. Overall, the relationship between age and activity is not perfectly linear.

## 24-Hour Activity Patterns

```{r nhanes-hourly-summary}
nhanes_hourly = nhanes_long |>
  group_by(education, sex, minute) |>
  summarize(
    mean_mims = mean(mims, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    hour = minute / 60
  )
```

```{r nhanes-hourly-plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
nhanes_hourly |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = hour,
    y = mean_mims,
    color = sex
  )) +
  geom_smooth(
    se = FALSE,
    span = 0.12
  ) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 24, 4),
    limits = c(0, 24)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "24-Hour Activity Patterns",
    x = "Hour of Day",
    y = "Average Activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
Activity levels are lowest during the early morning 3–5 AM, and increase rapidly after 6 AM. Activity remains higher during the daytime and decreases in the evening. The three education groups show similar daily patterns, and males and females have some differences in activity levels throughout the day.
# Problem 3
## Data import and cleaning


```{r citibike-import}
bike_files = list.files(
  "data/citibike",
  pattern = "\\.csv$",
  full.names = TRUE
)

citibike = purrr::map_dfr(
  bike_files,
  function(file) {
    read_csv(file, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
      janitor::clean_names() |>
      mutate(
        year = as.integer(
          str_extract(basename(file), "20[0-9]{2}")
        ),
        month = if_else(
          str_detect(basename(file), "Jan"),
          "January",
          "July"
        )
      )
  }
) |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(
      month,
      levels = c("January", "July")
    ),
    weekdays = factor(
      weekdays,
      levels = c(
        "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday",
        "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"
      )
    ),
    member_casual = factor(
      member_casual,
      levels = c("casual", "member")
    )
  )

dim(citibike)
head(citibike)
```
The Citi Bike dataset contains rides from January and July in 2020 and 2024. It includes information about bike type, membership status, day of the week, ride duration, and starting and ending stations. The data were combined into one dataset, with year and month added for each ride.

## Ride Counts by Year and Month

```{r citibike-counts}
citibike |>
  count(year, month, member_casual) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "Number of Rides by Year, Month, and Membership"
  )
```
Members took more rides than casual riders in both years. July had more rides than January in both 2020 and 2024. The number of rides was also higher in 2024 than in 2020, with July 2024 having the highest number of rides.
## Most Popular Starting Stations

```{r citibike-stations}
citibike |>
  filter(year == 2024, month == "July") |>
  count(start_station_name, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 5) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Starting Station", "Number of Rides"),
    caption = "Top Five Starting Stations in July 2024"
  )
```
## Median Ride Duration

```{r citibike-median-plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
citibike |>
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |>
  summarize(
    median_duration = median(duration, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = weekdays,
    y = median_duration,
    color = month,
    group = month
  )) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  facet_grid(. ~ year) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Ride Duration by Day of Week",
    x = "Day of Week",
    y = "Median Ride Duration (minutes)",
    color = "Month"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 45,
      hjust = 1
    )
  )
```
Median ride duration was longer in July than in January for both 2020 and 2024. In 2020, ride duration increased noticeably on weekends, especially in July. In 2024, weekend rides were also slightly longer, but the differences were smaller. Overall, median ride durations were higher in 2020 than in 2024.
## Ride Duration Distribution in 2024

```{r citibike-duration-plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
citibike |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = rideable_type,
    y = duration,
    fill = rideable_type
  )) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.1) +
  facet_grid(member_casual ~ month) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 60)) +
  labs(
    title = "Ride Duration Distribution in 2024",
    x = "Bike Type",
    y = "Ride Duration (minutes)",
    fill = "Bike Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Casual riders generally had longer rides than members in both January and July. Among casual riders, classic bikes had higher median ride durations than electric bikes. For members, electric bike rides were generally longer, especially in July. Ride durations also showed considerable variation, with many outliers.
